nameStory: The 'stork's-bill' name comes from the plant's distinctive long, pointed seed pods that look remarkably like a stork's beak! When the seeds are ripe, these 'bills' actually twist and spiral open in a corkscrew motion, flinging the seeds away from the parent plant. The 'redstem' part refers to the reddish coloring often seen on the stems, especially as the plant matures.
description: Redstem stork's-bill is a low-growing annual herb that spreads in small rosettes close to the ground. The plant rarely grows taller than 6-12 inches, with delicate, finely divided leaves that look almost feathery or carrot-like. It produces tiny pink to purple flowers with five petals, followed by its signature long, pointed seed pods. This European native has made itself at home across New England, often appearing in disturbed soils and sunny spots.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The unmistakable long, needle-like seed pods (1-2 inches) that look exactly like a stork's beak - this is the plant's calling card and will twist spirally when ripe

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, feathery leaves that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, arranged in small rosettes that hug the ground

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pink to purple flowers (about 1/2 inch across) with five rounded petals and visible veining, often appearing in small clusters

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading annual that forms small mats or rosettes, rarely getting taller than your hand, with stems that often show reddish coloring

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: When crushed, the leaves have a slightly sharp, geranium-like scent since this plant belongs to the geranium family

habitat: Look for redstem stork's-bill in disturbed soils, vacant lots, roadsides, gardens, and other sunny, open areas throughout New England. It thrives in poor, sandy, or gravelly soils where other plants struggle, and is commonly found around sidewalk cracks, parking lots, and construction sites. This adaptable plant prefers full sun and well-drained conditions.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge early and begin flowering in late spring, with the characteristic feathery leaves forming low rosettes. Look for the first tiny pink flowers starting in May.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering and seed production occurs through summer, when you'll see the distinctive stork's-bill seed pods developing and eventually spiraling open to release seeds.
seasonality.fall: Plants may continue flowering into early fall if conditions are favorable, with mature plants showing more pronounced red stem coloring before dying back.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, the plant dies completely in winter, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: The seed pods don't just look like stork bills - they actually act like tiny drill bits! When they hit the ground, changes in humidity cause them to twist and untwist repeatedly, literally screwing the seeds into the soil for perfect planting depth.
confusionNotes: The feathery leaves might be confused with young wild carrot (Queen Anne's lace), but stork's-bill stays much smaller, has pink flowers instead of white, and most importantly has those unmistakable long seed pods that wild carrot lacks.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'stork's-bill,' this plant is actually in the geranium family, not related to storks at all! It's also sometimes called 'filaree' from the Spanish word for 'little thread,' referring to the thin, thread-like seed pods.
compareHints: Redstem stork's-bill is the only Erodium species commonly found in New England, but it can be distinguished from its geranium family cousins (true geraniums) by its much smaller size, more finely divided leaves, and especially those characteristic long, pointed seed pods. True geraniums have rounded, less divided leaves and different seed structures.
